# M51 — Whirlpool Galaxy, the Question Mark

The Whirlpool Galaxy (M51) with its companion NGC 5195, framed in the
orientation that makes the pair read as a cosmic question mark — the
grand-design spiral forms the curl, and the companion galaxy dots it. The two
are in the middle of a close encounter: the bridge of gas and dust connecting
them is real tidal debris, and the gravitational tug of NGC 5195 is what winds
M51's spiral arms so dramatically. They sit about 30 million light-years away
in Canes Venatici, just below the handle of the Big Dipper.

Captured June 21, 2026. Also [on AstroBin](https://app.astrobin.com/i/qdwtrx).

- **Coordinates**: RA 13h 29m 53s, Dec +47° 11′ 43″ (Canes Venatici)
- **Optics**: Celestron EdgeHD 9.25 (C925)
- **Camera**: ZWO ASI2600MM Pro (mono)
- **Mount**: Sky-Watcher Wave 150i

# M31 — Andromeda and Friends

The Andromeda Galaxy and its entourage — M32 tucked against the disk and
M110 floating below. At 2.5 million light-years it's the nearest major galaxy
to our own, on course to merge with the Milky Way in about four billion
years. This one is a speed run: just one hour total, built from hundreds of
15-second RGB subs — a demonstration of how far fast optics and a modern CMOS
sensor can get on a bright target.

- **Coordinates**: RA 00h 42m 44s, Dec +41° 16′ 09″ (Andromeda)
- **Optics**: William Optics SpaceCat 61
- **Camera**: ZWO ASI2600MM Pro
- **Mount**: Sky-Watcher Wave 150i
- **Filters**: Baader R/G/B (CCD), 36 mm
- **Integration**: 1h — R 20m (80 × 15″), G 20m (80 × 15″), B 20m (80 × 15″)
- **Published**: 2025-08-02 — [on AstroBin](https://app.astrobin.com/i/ask6js)

# NGC 7331 and Stephan's Quintet

Two showpieces of Pegasus in one field. NGC 7331 — the anchor of the "Deer
Lick Group" — is a graceful flocculent spiral about 40 million light-years
away, once considered a twin of the Milky Way; the smaller galaxies scattered
behind it are ten times more distant, a chance line-of-sight grouping. In the
same frame sits Stephan's Quintet, the first compact galaxy group ever
discovered (1877): four of its five members are locked in a slow-motion
collision some 290 million light-years out.

- **Coordinates**: RA 22h 37m 04s, Dec +34° 24′ 56″ (Pegasus)
- **Optics**: Askar 107PHQ
- **Camera**: ZWO ASI2600MM DUO
- **Mount**: Sky-Watcher Wave 150i
- **Filters**: Baader LRGB (CMOS-optimized), 2 in
- **Published**: 2025-09-11 — [on AstroBin](https://app.astrobin.com/i/45gc9z)

# Sadr Region — Butterfly Nebula (IC 1318)

The heart of Cygnus. IC 1318, the Butterfly Nebula, spreads its two glowing
wings across this field, split down the middle by the dark dust lane LDN 889.
The bright haloed star near the bottom is Sadr (γ Cygni) itself, the center
star of the Northern Cross — a foreground supergiant about 1,800 light-years
away, with the nebulosity roughly twice as far behind it. Rendered in a
golden SHO-style narrowband palette. File dated July 27, 2025.

- **Coordinates**: RA 20h 22m 14s, Dec +40° 15′ 24″ (Cygnus)
- **Camera**: ZWO ASI2600MM Pro
- **Mount**: Sky-Watcher Wave 150i
- **Captured**: circa late July 2025

# IC 1396 — Elephant's Trunk Nebula (Widefield)

IC 1396 in Cepheus, a vast emission complex about 2,400 light-years away,
with the famous Elephant's Trunk — a dense globule of gas and dust being
eroded and lit from behind by the hot O-star at the cluster's heart — winding
through the middle. The trunk is a stellar nursery: infrared surveys have
found protostars forming inside it. Shot over five nights in early August
2025 through 3nm narrowband filters, 11½ hours total, and processed with a
Foraxx palette.

- **Coordinates**: RA 21h 39m 06s, Dec +57° 30′ (Cepheus)
- **Optics**: William Optics SpaceCat 61
- **Camera**: ZWO ASI2600MM Pro
- **Mount**: Sky-Watcher Wave 150i
- **Filters**: Antlia 3nm Hα / OIII / SII, 36 mm
- **Integration**: 11h 30m — Hα 3h 50m (46 × 300″), SII 3h 50m (46 × 300″), OIII 3h 50m (46 × 300″)
- **Published**: 2025-09-03 — [on AstroBin](https://app.astrobin.com/i/187h12)

# Sh2-92 — The Scream (Widefield)

Sh2-92, nicknamed "The Scream" for the anguished face that emerges in
narrowband renders — a faint, rarely imaged H II region in Vulpecula. It's a
genuinely big object: a cavity over 200 light-years across, roughly 14,000
light-years away, blown open and ionized by the Wolf-Rayet star WR 127. Six
and a quarter hours of 3nm narrowband, processed with a Foraxx palette.

- **Coordinates**: RA 19h 47m, Dec +28° 15′ (Vulpecula)
- **Optics**: William Optics SpaceCat 61
- **Camera**: ZWO ASI2600MM Pro
- **Mount**: Sky-Watcher Wave 150i

- **Integration**: 6h 15m — Hα 2h 5m (25 × 300″), SII 2h 5m (25 × 300″), OIII 2h 5m (25 × 300″)
- **Published**: 2025-08-21 — [on AstroBin](https://app.astrobin.com/i/p35ii5)

# M33 — Triangulum Galaxy (HaLRGB)

M33, the Triangulum Galaxy — at 2.7 million light-years the third-largest
member of our Local Group, and faintly visible to the naked eye from a truly
dark site. The Hα layer in this HaLRGB blend makes its star-forming regions
pop as red knots along the arms, including NGC 604, one of the largest known
stellar nurseries anywhere. Four hours of short 15-second LRGB subs keep the
core clean, with 80 minutes of 3nm Hα layered on top.

- **Coordinates**: RA 01h 33m 51s, Dec +30° 39′ 37″ (Triangulum)
- **Optics**: Askar 107PHQ
- **Camera**: ZWO ASI2600MM DUO
- **Mount**: Sky-Watcher Wave 150i
- **Filters**: Baader LRGB + UV/IR-cut (CMOS-optimized), 2 in; Antlia 3nm Hα, 2 in
- **Integration**: 5h 20m — L 1h (240 × 15″), R 1h (240 × 15″), G 1h (240 × 15″), B 1h (240 × 15″), Hα 1h 20m (16 × 300″)
- **Published**: 2025-08-21 — [on AstroBin](https://app.astrobin.com/i/6w48vg)

# Comet C/2025 A6 (Lemmon)

Comet C/2025 A6 (Lemmon), the standout comet of late 2025. Discovered in
January 2025 by the Mount Lemmon Survey, it brightened far beyond predictions
and became a naked-eye object in the October evening sky. This RGB capture is
from October 20, 2025 — right around its closest approach to Earth — with the
ion tail streaming away from the coma. No fixed coordinates for this one: it
was moving fast enough between frames that the stars and comet have to be
stacked separately.

- **Optics**: William Optics SpaceCat 61
- **Camera**: ZWO ASI2600MM Pro
- **Mount**: Sky-Watcher Wave 150i
- **Filters**: Baader R/G/B (CCD), 36 mm
- **Published**: 2025-10-20 — [on AstroBin](https://app.astrobin.com/i/fke4gn)

# NGC 6888 — Crescent Nebula

The Crescent Nebula in Cygnus, about 5,000 light-years away — a shell of gas
thrown off by the Wolf-Rayet star WR 136 and now being slammed from behind by
the star's own faster wind. The collision lights up the delicate blue-green
OIII envelope that wraps the whole crescent like a soap bubble, floating over
a field of red hydrogen. Rendered in a narrowband bicolor palette that keeps
that OIII shell front and center. File dated August 7, 2025.

- **Coordinates**: RA 20h 12m 06s, Dec +38° 21′ 18″ (Cygnus)
- **Camera**: ZWO ASI2600MM Pro
- **Mount**: Sky-Watcher Wave 150i
- **Captured**: circa early August 2025

# WR 134 — Wolf-Rayet Bubble (Widefield)

WR 134 in Cygnus, a Wolf-Rayet star roughly 6,000 light-years away — a
massive star in its final act, shedding its outer layers in a ferocious wind.
The ghostly blue OIII arc is the edge of a wind-blown bubble where that
material slams into gas the star expelled earlier in its life. The OIII
signal is what makes this target, so it got an extra 50 minutes: 8h 20m of
3nm narrowband in total.

- **Coordinates**: RA 20h 10m 14s, Dec +36° 10′ 35″ (Cygnus)
- **Optics**: William Optics SpaceCat 61
- **Camera**: ZWO ASI2600MM Pro
- **Mount**: Sky-Watcher Wave 150i
- **Filters**: Antlia 3nm Hα / OIII / SII, 36 mm
- **Integration**: 8h 20m — Hα 2h 30m (30 × 300″), SII 2h 30m (30 × 300″), OIII 3h 20m (40 × 300″)
- **Published**: 2025-08-03 — [on AstroBin](https://app.astrobin.com/i/a3hd7c)

# C33 / C34 — The Wider Veil Nebulas

The Veil Nebula complex in Cygnus — the shredded remains of a star that
exploded ten to twenty thousand years ago, now a lacework of shock fronts
some 2,400 light-years away and six full moons wide. This widefield takes in
both the Eastern Veil (C33) and the Western Veil (C34) with Pickering's
Triangle between them, in two quick hours of narrowband.

- **Coordinates**: RA 20h 51m, Dec +30° 40′ (Cygnus)
- **Optics**: Radian 61
- **Camera**: ZWO ASI2600MM Pro
- **Mount**: Sky-Watcher Wave 150i
- **Filters**: Optolong Hα 7nm / OIII 6.5nm / SII 6.5nm; Baader R/G/B (CMOS-optimized), 36 mm
- **Integration**: 2h — Hα 40m (8 × 300″), SII 40m (8 × 300″), OIII 40m (16 × 150″)
- **Published**: 2025-07-29 — [on AstroBin](https://app.astrobin.com/i/wuv24k)

# Sh2-101 — The Tulip Field

The Tulip Nebula, Sh2-101, blooming in Cygnus about 6,000 light-years away —
an emission region sculpted into petals by radiation from young O-type stars.
The same field hides one of the sky's most famous invisible objects: Cygnus
X-1, the first widely accepted black hole, whose jet inflates a faint shock
bubble near the Tulip. 11½ hours of 3nm narrowband across Hα, SII, and
OIII.

- **Coordinates**: RA 19h 59m 55s, Dec +35° 16′ 35″ (Cygnus)
- **Optics**: William Optics SpaceCat 61
- **Camera**: ZWO ASI2600MM Pro
- **Mount**: Sky-Watcher Wave 150i

# SN 2026sqf — Supernova in NGC 3310

A brand-new supernova, caught two days after discovery. SN 2026sqf was
discovered on July 8, 2026 by Patrick Wiggins in NGC 3310, and quickly
classified as a Type II — the core collapse of a massive star that has run out
of fuel. At capture it was shining around magnitude 13, remarkably bright for
a supernova, sitting as a distinct point of light about half an arcminute from
the galaxy's nucleus, just outside the bright disk.

The host, NGC 3310 (Arp 217), is a grand-design starburst spiral in Ursa
Major, roughly 50 million light-years away — the light from this explosion
left before the first grass evolved on Earth. Its furious star formation,
likely triggered by swallowing a satellite galaxy ~100 million years ago,
makes it a repeat supernova producer.

These frames were shot in a hurry at sunset on July 10, 2026 — twilight still
brightening the sky — as 8 stacked frames through an LRGB chroma filter. Two renders: one labeled
with the supernova circled, and a normal processed version.

- **Supernova**: RA 10h 38m 47.9s, Dec +53° 30′ 34″ (Ursa Major)
- **Host galaxy**: NGC 3310, RA 10h 38m 45.9s, Dec +53° 30′ 12″
- **Optics**: Celestron EdgeHD 9.25 (C925)
- **Camera**: ZWO ASI2600MM (mono), LRGB chroma filter, 8 frames stacked
- **Captured**: 2026-07-10, at sunset

# DWB 111 — Propeller Nebula Region

The Propeller Nebula (DWB 111 / Simeis 57) and its surroundings in northern
Cygnus — a strange S-shaped twist of hydrogen whose origin still isn't
settled, embedded in a huge field of glowing filaments, with faint blue-green
OIII arcs threading through the red. Two takes here: an early
portrait-orientation render from late July 2025, and a wider September 2025
revisit with the SpaceCat 61.

- **Coordinates**: RA 20h 16m 12s, Dec +43° 41′ (Cygnus)
- **Camera**: ZWO ASI2600MM Pro
- **Mount**: Sky-Watcher Wave 150i
- **Captured**: July and September 2025

# Sh2-119 — The Clamshell Nebula

Sh2-119, the Clamshell Nebula — the North America Nebula's overlooked
next-door neighbor, sitting just east of it in Cygnus around the naked-eye
star 68 Cygni. It rarely gets imaged on its own, which is a shame: in
narrowband its interleaved shells and dark lanes have real depth. Five hours
of narrowband with short RGB runs for natural star color, processed with a
Foraxx palette.

- **Coordinates**: RA 21h 18m, Dec +43° 57′ (Cygnus)
- **Optics**: Radian 61
- **Camera**: ZWO ASI2600MM Pro
- **Mount**: Sky-Watcher Wave 150i
- **Filters**: Optolong Hα 7nm / OIII 6.5nm / SII 6.5nm; Baader R/G/B (CMOS-optimized), 36 mm
- **Integration**: 5h 10m — R/G/B 13m 20s each (40 × 20″), Hα 1h 20m (16 × 300″), SII 1h 20m (16 × 300″), OIII 1h 50m (22 × 300″)
- **Published**: 2025-07-27 — [on AstroBin](https://app.astrobin.com/i/clsirc)

# NGC 7000 — North America Nebula (2025-07)

The North America Nebula, a sprawling emission nebula in Cygnus about 2,600
light-years away, its familiar continent shape carved out by dark foreground
dust along the "Gulf of Mexico" region. Captured July 19, 2025 in narrowband
with a monochrome camera; two renders here: an HOO-palette combination
(hydrogen-alpha and doubly-ionized oxygen) and a stretched PixelMath blend.

- **Coordinates**: RA 20h 59m 17s, Dec +44° 31′ 44″ (Cygnus)
- **Optics**: Celestron EdgeHD 9.25 (C925)
- **Camera**: ZWO ASI2600MM Pro (mono), narrowband filters
- **Captured**: 2025-07-19
